pattern: no Rust-written file: Python's intents name parts the Rust engine does not have
evidence: NIST CTC-02 and CTC-04: OpenCascade's XCAF makes a part of each shape representation of one product (the solid and its surface models: 3 and 2 parts), haecceity one part per product with all its faces (question Q7; existing.json and the part stream's entries). Python's accept-defaults intents are bound to parts 1 and 2 of its numbering, which the Rust engine's reading of the file does not have, so examples/write_fixtures.rs refuses the case before calling the writer (its part-index check; the message is rust.refused.txt) rather than write an intent onto the wrong part; Python itself refuses the write of these files ('this assembly already has PMI not written by specify-core', write.json). Nothing to cross until Q7 is settled; an intent made by the Rust engine's own analysis of these files is the CLI stream's to write.

path: python_readback[specify-core's process died with SIGSEGV in load.load_all]
pattern: OpenCascade 7.9 crashes opening a Rust-written file with datum feature symbols
evidence: Every Rust-written synthetic file with a datum (7 of the 11: plate, pin, stack, assembly, a_hole_along_x, four_corner_holes, identical_holes) kills specify-core's process with SIGSEGV in load.load_all (STEPCAFControl_Reader), captured in a child process by tools/capture/crossengine.py; the 4 without datums (a_file_with_two_parts, a_placed_part, default_datum_a, wrapped) and both NIST files, written in add mode on their own datums with no symbols added, load. The cause is the one MECHANICAL_DESIGN_AND_DRAUGHTING_RELATIONSHIP('','',#shape representation,#'datum feature symbols' DRAUGHTING_MODEL) haecceity writes for its datum symbols (docs/upstream-needs.md U15): with it removed every file loads (python_readback_without_symbols.json.gz, the capture's probe), and with rep_1 and rep_2 swapped the plate still crashes (checked by hand). The form is schema-valid as far as checked: the relationship's rep_1/rep_2 select (mechanical_design_and_draughting_relationship_select) admits shape_representation, the shared context satisfies its supertype, and haecceity's instance validation passes; its WR1-WR3 are not evaluated by haecceity (express_rules.rs does not list them) and were not checked here. All six NIST CAx-IF files (tests/fixtures/nist) use this relationship only between two DRAUGHTING_MODELs (saved views), never with a shape representation. A reader crashing is OpenCascade's defect whatever the form; whether the form is the PMI practice's is not established, and leaving it out is question Q16. Until then no file the Rust engine writes with a datum opens in specify-core (Python) or any OpenCascade 7.9 tool.

pattern: a thread written as AP242's thread feature is not read by specify-core (Python)
evidence: The Rust writer writes each thread as AP242's `thread` (side, major diameter, form, class, hand, partial area; haecceity checks thread WR1-WR16 on every write) with its pitch and depths as a user defined attribute set (UDA practice §5-7; upstream need U8), and reads it back as the intent's thread. specify-core's existing.notes reads threads only from its own 'manufacturing requirement' text route (existing.py, notes), and OpenCascade's XCAF has no thread model, so Python reads none of them (6 threads in the probes of plate, pin, stack, assembly and a_hole_along_x). The AP242 schema form is standard, the text route is not (haecceity decision 5), but no CAx-IF practice for thread features was found to cite, and the pitch has no semantic home in haecceity yet (U8). A thread therefore does not cross from the Rust engine to the Python one.

pattern: a size or tolerance on a feature of several faces (set_representation_item) is not read by OpenCascade
evidence: Each missing item is on a feature of several faces (a hole pattern's or a hole set's cylinders: NIST CTC-03's Ø4.7625 H11 and its position 0.76 MMC on the 8 faces of hole_patterns.rectangle, the plate's and assembly's Ø6.6 hole set, the four corner holes, the identical holes, the stack's tapped set), which haecceity writes as one SHAPE_ASPECT with an ITEM_IDENTIFIED_REPRESENTATION_USAGE whose identified_item is a SET_REPRESENTATION_ITEM of the faces (e.g. CTC-03 rust.step #6002): the PMI practice's §6.5.1 form, allowed by AP242's item_identified_representation_usage_select (list_representation_item, representation_item, set_representation_item). OpenCascade's reader does not resolve such a usage to faces and drops the size and the tolerance on it (haecceity's own tools/check_pmi_occt.py reports the same, docs/step-ap242.md). The same sizes and tolerances on a single face read (the plate's position on its tapped hole, the stack's Ø8 bore).

pattern: a datum is read by OpenCascade only through a tolerance it reads
evidence: four_corner_holes and identical_holes: datums A, B and C are written as on the plate (one `datum` per letter with its `datum_feature` on the faces, practice §6.5), and the plate's datums do read (its position on face 12 cites them). specify-core reads datums from XCAF's datum labels (existing.py, GetDatumLabels), which OpenCascade's reader makes from the datum systems of the tolerances it reads; on these two parts the only tolerance citing A|B|C is the position on the hole set, a feature of several faces it does not read (the set_representation_item entry), so it never reaches the datums. Not a defect of the written datums.

pattern: a fit written as its ISO 286 class reads with no limits in specify-core (Python)
evidence: The stack's Ø8 H7 bores ([9] of parts 0 and 1, +0.015/0) and Ø8 h6 pin ([3] of part 2, 0/-0.009) read back in Python with their nominal value and no upper or lower deviation. The Rust writer writes a fit as plus_minus_tolerance -> limits_and_fits('H','hole','7','') (PMI practice §5.2.5), after checking the intent's limits are the class's (src/writer.rs); haecceity's reader reads the class. specify-core's read_existing takes limits only from IsDimWithPlusMinusTolerance (existing.py) and never asks XCAF for the class of tolerance, so the fit's meaning is lost on the Python side. Python's own files carry the fit as bare limits, which is what OCCT's writer forced (docs/design.md, 'What is written').

path: *resume[python did not resume: fingerprint differs only in signs of zero]
pattern: Python finds the Rust-written answers but refuses them on the fingerprint: zeros' signs differ
evidence: On every Rust-written part Python could load (the 2 parts of a_file_with_two_parts, a_placed_part, default_datum_a, wrapped; and every part of the probes) the capture's resume evidence shows Python's pattern (resume.saved) finds exactly the payload the Rust writer stored, with the same face count, and the faces Python fingerprints equal the Rust engine's in kind and rounded centroid by value; only the signs of some zero components differ (OpenCascade -0.0, haecceity 0.0: integration noise), which Python's json.dumps text and so the sha256 keep. Checked per part by tests/cross_engine.rs (faces_gap). Neither engine's zero is more correct; the payload format hashes text. Question Q14: the answers do not cross until the fingerprint writes zeros unsigned or the rule changes.

path: python_written.resume[rust did not resume: fingerprint differs only in signs of zero]
pattern: the Rust engine finds Python-written answers but refuses them on the fingerprint: zeros' signs differ
evidence: On every part of the 11 Python-written synthetic files (tests/fixtures/oracle/parts/**/written.step.gz) resume::stored reads Python's payload, equal to what Python's own resume.saved finds (python_written_evidence.json.gz), with the same face count; the stored fingerprint is Python's hash of the faces it lists, and those faces equal the Rust engine's by value, differing only in signs of zero (faces_gap). Everything else these files hold (existing PMI, part settings) reads in Rust exactly as Python reads it. The same cause as the other direction: question Q14.
